newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Spanish King meets Yeltsin, Russian Patriarch.
newsitem.headline: Spanish King meets Yeltsin, Russian Patriarch.

text.p: Spain's King Juan Carlos met Russian President Boris Yeltsin in the Kremlin on Tuesday for talks touching on economic ties and the vexed issue of NATO's eastward expansion.
"We have many important problems to discuss," Yeltsin told reporters before ushering his royal guest into private talks.

A Spanish official said Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes had tried, like a string of western leaders before him, to convince Yeltsin that NATO's plan to invite in new members at a meeting in Madrid in July was not directed against Russia.
Yeltsin reiterated his firm opposition to NATO expansion at the meeting, said the official from the Spanish delegation.
The king is on a three-day state visit, his second to Moscow but his first since the collapse of communist rule in Russia.
His role is largely ceremonial but he has brought with him dozens of Spanish business representatives to try to foster mutual trade and investment in Russia's post-communist economy.

At a meeting of Russia's chamber of commerce, First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemstov told the king a new tax code he and his reform-oriented government colleagues were planning would make foreign investment in Russia a more attractive prospect.

Later on Tuesday Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia met Patriarch Alexiy II, head of the Russian Orthodox Church, who showed them around the Assumption Cathedral, where Russian Tsars were buried before the Bolshevik revolution.

Alexiy told them the church was now free after 70 years of communist oppression. Juan Carlos said he was glad of the opportunity to learn more about the church and invited the Patriarch to visit Spain.
Juan Carlos will open an exhibition of Spanish art on Wednesday at Moscow's Pushkin Museum, to include paintings by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miro and Salvador Dali.

Russian media have given the royal visit prominent coverage, drawing parallels between Spain's transition to democracy since the 1970s under Juan Carlos's supervision and their own country's passage from communism to a free society.
The liberal daily newspaper Sevodnya said Juan Carlos had much to teach his Russian hosts in the art of uniting and reconciling a divided nation.
Russia and Spain signed a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation in 1994 but are keen to increase trade, which Itar-Tass news agency said rose almost 50 percent last year to $1.87 billion.

Moscow's main export to Spain is oil and oil products, while Spain exports foodstuffs to Russia. Tass said trade ministry officials predict an increase in Spanish exports of meat, edible oils, fruit and vegetables this year.
